  "rubric": "# Marking Rubric — Performance Optimization I Assessment\n\n**Total: 100 points**\n\n---\n\n## Section A — Tree-Shaking (35 points)\n\n### Q1 — Definition & Module Format (8 points)\n\n**Full marks (8):**\n- Clearly defines tree-shaking as dead code elimination — removing exported code that is never imported/used, resulting in a smaller production bundle.\n- Identifies the problem: JavaScript-heavy apps accumulate unused code from libraries/dependencies that bloats bundles and slows load times.\n- Correctly explains the 'tree' metaphor: the dependency graph is the tree; shaking it drops dead branches (unused exports/modules).\n- Specifies ES2015 (ES6) `import`/`export` (ESM) syntax as required.\n- Correctly explains *why*: ESM imports are *static* and *top-level* — the bundler can analyze exactly what is used at build time without executing code; CommonJS `require()` is dynamic and can appear anywhere (conditionally, inside functions), making static analysis impossible or unreliable.\n\n**Partial (4–7):** Defines tree-shaking correctly and names ESM but gives an incomplete or vague explanation of why static structure matters; or correctly explains everything except the CommonJS comparison.\n\n**Minimal (1–3):** Shows a basic awareness ('removes unused code') but cannot explain the module format requirement or the static vs. dynamic distinction.\n\n**Zero (0):** Incorrect or blank.\n\n---\n\n### Q2 — Transfer Size vs. Actual Size (10 points)\n\n**Full marks (10):**\n\n**Part a (5):** Explains that compression (gzip/brotli) only reduces *transfer size*; once the browser receives the file, it must decompress it, then parse, compile, and execute the full JavaScript — all of which takes CPU time proportional to the actual uncompressed size, not the transfer size. The parser and compiler see 900 KB of JS even if it was 300 KB on the wire.\n\n**Part b (5):** Identifies the flaw in the developer's reasoning: 300 KB gzipped could be ~900 KB or more after decompression. The performance cost (parse/compile/execute) scales with the *decompressed* size. Simply citing a compressed size does not characterize the real performance burden on lower-powered devices. The student should recommend measuring and communicating *uncompressed* size and/or actual parse/compile time.\n\n**Partial:** Correctly addresses one part fully and the other partially. Award proportionally.\n\n**Minimal:** Understands compression is involved but cannot articulate the parse/compile step or the distinction's practical meaning.\n\n---\n\n### Q3 — `sideEffects` & `/*#__PURE__*/` (10 points)\n\n**Full marks (10):**\n\n**Part a (4):** A *side effect* is code that performs behavior when a module is *imported* beyond just providing exports — e.g., modifying global state, registering event listeners, patching `Array.prototype`, or writing to `window`.\n- Good example **with** side effect: a polyfill (e.g., `import 'core-js/stable'`) that patches global objects; a CSS import that injects styles.\n- Good example **without** side effect: a pure utility module that only exports functions like `add(a, b)` or `formatDate(date)`.\n\n**Part b (4):** Setting `\"sideEffects\": false` tells webpack it is safe to prune any export from that package that is not explicitly used — the entire module can be dropped if nothing from it is imported. Risk: if a module *does* have side effects (e.g., a polyfill file), marking it false means webpack may drop it from the bundle even though it was needed, causing runtime breakage — missing globals, missing patches, etc.\n\n**Part c (2):** `/*#__PURE__*/` is an inline annotation on a function call (typically a higher-order function call or class instantiation) that tells Terser/the minifier the call is side-effect-free, so the entire statement can be removed if its return value is unused. It is a per-call safety signal, complementing the module-level `sideEffects` field.\n\n**Partial:** Correctly handles two of the three parts; award ~7/10. One part handled well: ~4/10.\n\n---\n\n### Q4 — Babel Configuration & Other Tree-Shaking Mistakes (7 points)\n\n**Full marks (7):**\n\n**Part a (2):** Babel (via `@babel/preset-env`) by default transforms ES module `import`/`export` statements into CommonJS `require()`/`module.exports`. This destroys the static structure that webpack needs for tree-shaking, so the bundler cannot determine what is unused.\n\n**Part b (3):** Setting `\"modules\": false` in the Babel preset config (inside `.babelrc` or `babel.config.js`) tells Babel to leave `import`/`export` statements untransformed, preserving the ESM static structure for webpack to analyze.\n\nExample: `[\"@babel/preset-env\", { \"modules\": false }]`\n\n**Part c (2):** Any one reasonable alternative failure mode, e.g.:\n- Using a namespace import (`import * as utils from './utils'`) with dynamic property access like `utils[key]()` — webpack cannot statically determine which exports are used.\n- Importing from a library that ships only CommonJS (`module.exports = {...}`).\n- Using a default export that is an object containing methods — all methods travel together; only named exports are individually shakeable.\n- Not running in `mode: 'production'` (which activates `optimization.usedExports` and Terser).\n\n**Partial:** Correctly identifies Babel as the problem but cannot specify the fix, or identifies the fix but not the mechanism. Part c blank: subtract 2.\n\n---\n\n## Section B — Event Bubbling & Capturing (35 points)\n\n### Q5 — Three Phases of Event Propagation (8 points)\n\n**Full marks (8):**\n- **Capturing phase:** Event travels from `window` down through ancestors to the target element. A listener attached with `{ capture: true }` (or `addEventListener(type, fn, true)`) fires during this phase. Use case: intercepting events before they reach deeply nested elements (e.g., global logging, access control).\n- **Target phase:** Event reaches the element that was originally interacted with (`event.target`). Both capturing and bubbling listeners on the target itself may fire.\n- **Bubbling phase:** Event travels back up from the target through ancestors to `window`. This is the default phase for `addEventListener` with no third argument (or `false`). Most everyday event handling occurs here; enables event delegation.\n\nMust name all three phases correctly, give the correct direction for each, and give a plausible use case for at least capturing and bubbling.\n\n**Partial (4–7):** Names and describes two phases correctly; or names all three but confuses direction or use case.\n\n**Minimal (1–3):** Knows bubbling only; cannot name capturing or the target phase.\n\n---\n\n### Q6 — Bubbling Order, stopPropagation, stopImmediatePropagation (9 points)\n\n**Full marks (9):**\n\n**Part a (3):** Bubbling order from the click on `#inner`:\n1. `#inner` (button) — target\n2. `#middle` (div)\n3. `#outer` (div)\n4. `<body>` → `<html>` → `document` → `window`\n\nAt minimum: `#inner` → `#middle` → `#outer` must be listed in correct order.\n\n**Part b (3):** `event.stopPropagation()` called on `#outer` stops the event from bubbling further up (to `<body>`, `document`, `window`). It does **not** prevent other listeners already registered on `#outer` itself from firing; it also does not prevent the event's default browser action (e.g., following a link).\n\n**Part c (3):** `event.stopImmediatePropagation()` stops propagation *and* prevents any further listeners on the **same element** from firing (if multiple handlers are attached to the same element for the same event). \n\nDifference: `stopPropagation` allows other listeners on the current element to still run; `stopImmediatePropagation` prevents them too.\n\nUse-case for `stopImmediatePropagation`: when you need a handler on an element to be the absolute last one to respond, with no other co-registered handlers on that element executing.\n\n---\n\n### Q7 — Event Delegation (9 points)\n\n**Full marks (9):**\n\n**Part a (3):** Without delegation, you'd attach a listener to every child element individually — expensive in memory, and you must reattach listeners when new children are added dynamically. Delegation attaches one listener to a common ancestor; it handles events for all current and future children because those events bubble up.\n\n**Part b (3):** Use `event.target` — the element that originally dispatched the event (the actual element clicked). `event.currentTarget` points to the element the listener is attached to (the ancestor/delegate), which is always the same element and therefore does not tell you which child was clicked.\n\n**Part c (3):** Any one well-explained limitation:\n- Events that don't bubble (e.g., `focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter`, `mouseleave`) cannot be delegated with this pattern (use `focusin`/`focusout` instead, which do bubble).\n- You must check `event.target` carefully (e.g., with `.closest()`) because the click may land on a child element *inside* the intended target.\n- `stopPropagation()` called in a child handler will prevent the event from reaching the delegating ancestor, silently breaking delegation.\n\n---\n\n### Q8 — preventDefault, Non-bubbling Events, target vs. currentTarget (9 points)\n\n**Full marks (9):**\n\n**Part a (3):** `preventDefault()` cancels the browser's *default behavior* for the event (e.g., prevents a form from submitting to the server, prevents a link from navigating, prevents a checkbox from toggling). It does *not* stop propagation. `stopPropagation()` halts the event's travel through the DOM but does *not* affect the default action.\n\nConcrete examples: `preventDefault()` on a form `submit` event to handle submission via AJAX; `stopPropagation()` on a modal's click to prevent closing the modal when clicking inside it.\n\n**Part b (3):** Examples of non-bubbling events: `focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter`, `mouseleave`, `load`, `scroll` (on specific elements). Impact for delegation: you cannot delegate these events via bubbling to an ancestor in the usual way. You would need to either attach listeners directly to each element, or use the capturing phase, or use the bubbling equivalents (`focusin`/`focusout`).\n\n**Part c (3):** \n- `event.target`: the element that originally triggered the event (the deepest element clicked). Does not change as the event bubbles.\n- `event.currentTarget`: the element whose event listener is currently executing. Changes at each level as the event propagates up the DOM.\n\nIn a nested tree: if you click `#inner` and the event bubbles to `#outer`, a handler on `#outer` will see `event.target = #inner` and `event.currentTarget = #outer`.\n\n---\n\n## Section C — React Synthetic Events (30 points)\n\n### Q9 — What is a Synthetic Event & React's Event System (8 points)\n\n**Full marks (8):**\n\n**Part a (4):** A synthetic event is React's cross-browser wrapper around the browser's native event. It conforms to the W3C `Event` interface (same API: `stopPropagation`, `preventDefault`, `target`, etc.) so it behaves consistently across browsers. React created this abstraction to normalize browser inconsistencies and, historically, to enable event pooling and centralized event management.\n\n**Part b (4):** React does **not** attach individual listeners to each element. Instead, it attaches a single event listener (or very few) at the root of the React tree (e.g., the root DOM container). Events bubble up from the target to the root, where React intercepts them and dispatches synthetic events to the appropriate React component handlers. This is inherently an event delegation pattern and reduces the total number of DOM event listeners, improving memory usage especially in large component trees.\n\n**Partial:** Correctly describes what a synthetic event is but does not address the root-level delegation mechanism, or vice versa. Award 4/8.\n\n---\n\n### Q10 — Naming Conventions & Handler Passing (10 points)\n\n**Full marks (10):**\n\n**Part a (3):** By convention, event handler *props* for custom components are named starting with `on` followed by a capitalized event name — e.g., `onSubmit`, `onClick`, `onChange`. The handler function itself is conventionally named with a `handle` prefix — e.g., `handleClick`, `handleSubmit`. Native HTML attributes use lowercase like `onclick` (not used in JSX); in JSX the camelCase `onClick` maps to the underlying handler.\n\n**Part b (4):** \n- `<button onClick={handleClick}>` — passes the function *reference* to the `onClick` prop. React calls `handleClick` when the button is clicked. This is correct.\n- `<button onClick={handleClick()}>` — *invokes* `handleClick` immediately during render, and passes its *return value* (likely `undefined`) as the `onClick` prop. The click handler is effectively lost and the function runs on every render. This is a common bug.\n\n**Part c (3):** Any two from:\n- `event.target` / `event.currentTarget` — identifies the element involved.\n- `event.preventDefault()` — prevents default browser behavior (e.g., form submit, link navigation).\n- `event.stopPropagation()` — stops the event from bubbling further.\n- `event.type` — the type of event as a string (e.g., `'click'`).\n- `event.nativeEvent` — the underlying native browser event.\n\nAwarded 1.5 points per correct example with description.\n\n**Partial:** Correct on two of the three parts: ~7/10. One part: ~3–4/10.\n\n---\n\n### Q11 — Propagation, Prop Passing Pattern, preventDefault in React (12 points)\n\n**Full marks (12):**\n\n**Part a (3):** Call `e.stopPropagation()` on the synthetic event object — same method name as vanilla JavaScript. This stops the event from bubbling through the React component tree. The API is the same, though it is acting on the synthetic event wrapper. Note: React's synthetic events bubble through the React tree (component hierarchy), and since React roots its listeners at the DOM root, calling `stopPropagation` on a native event outside React may not stop the synthetic handler.\n\n**Part b (4):** Pattern: parent declares a function (e.g., `handleChildAction`) and passes it to the child as a prop (e.g., `onAction={handleChildAction}`). The child calls `props.onAction(data)` inside its own event handler. This lets the child communicate data/events *up* to the parent — the React equivalent of the classic 'lifting state up' / callback pattern — enabling unidirectional data flow.\n\n**Part c (5):**\n- `e.preventDefault()` in this context prevents the browser's default form submission behavior (which would cause a full page reload/GET or POST request to the server).\n- Without it, clicking Submit would still call `handleSubmit`, but the browser would *also* attempt a page reload/form POST, typically interrupting or overwriting any JavaScript handling.\n- `e` is a **React synthetic event** (an instance of React's `SyntheticEvent`), not a native browser event directly. Practically: it has the same API (`preventDefault`, `stopPropagation`, `target`, etc.) so developers use it identically; the difference is mostly internal — React normalizes behavior across browsers and handles the event through its root-level delegation system. Developers rarely need to access `e.nativeEvent` unless doing something unusual.\n\n**Partial:** Correctly handles two of the three sub-parts fully. Award ~8/12. One sub-part: ~4/12.\n\n---\n\n## Grading Summary\n\n| Section | Max Points |\n|---|---|\n| A — Tree-Shaking (Q1–Q4) | 35 |\n| B — Event Bubbling (Q5–Q8) | 35 |\n| C — React Synthetic Events (Q9–Q11) | 30 |\n| **Total** | **100** |\n\n**Score Bands:**\n- 90–100: Distinction — deep, accurate understanding across all three topics\n- 75–89: Merit — solid understanding with minor gaps\n- 60–74: Pass — foundational understanding; some conceptual gaps\n- Below 60: Needs review — revisit curriculum materials before progressing",
